title: Genetic code expansion enables plant-directed control of bacterial activity
projectDescription: Microbes have the potential to provide growth-promoting benefits to plants and crops, but effective plant–microbe partnerships require mechanisms to control microbial activity in a programmable and host-specific manner. Using O-methyl-L-tyrosine (OMY), a non-canonical amino acid (ncAA), as a model compound, we established a plant-based approach for controlling the activity of associated microbes. Arabidopsis thaliana plants engineered to produce OMY (proUBQ10::sfGFP-MfnG) exhibited reduced primary root length, decreased lateral root density, and impaired gravitropism compared with wild-type Col-0 plants. To investigate the basis of OMY-associated growth inhibition, we tested whether OMY phytotoxicity results from its misincorporation into endogenous proteins, a mechanism reported for other ncAAs. Specifically, we examined whether OMY-producing Arabidopsis plants accumulate O-methylated L-tyrosine residues in native proteins. Proteomic analysis was performed using shoot and root tissues from OMY-producing proUBQ10::sfGFP-MfnG plants and wild-type controls. The resulting proteomic data were analyzed to identify peptides containing O-methylated L-tyrosine residues and to determine whether their abundance was increased in OMY-producing plants relative to wild-type controls.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings were grown on 1× MS Gelzan plates and harvested at 14 days. Shoot and root tissues were separated, weighed, immediately flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C until protein extraction. Tissues were homogenized using a bead mill and extracted in 2× SDS sample loading buffer. Protein extracts were subjected to a short SDS- PAGE run, with buffer lanes between samples to minimize cross-contamination. For visualization, gels were stained for 6 h using a methanol-free colloidal blue staining solution to avoid potential artificial methylation during sample preparation and subsequently destained overnight with HPLC-grade water. Whole protein bands were excised and cut into approximately 1 mm² pieces for in-gel digestion. Gel pieces were extensively destained with ammonium bicarbonate/acetonitrile washes, followed by reduction with dithiothreitol at 56 °C for 1 h and alkylation with iodoacetamide in the dark at room temperature for 45 min. Gel pieces were  washed, dried, rehydrated with sequencing-grade trypsin in ammonium bicarbonate, and digested overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were extracted from the gel pieces using 50% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid, with three sequential extraction steps. Combined peptide extracts were centrifuged, dried by SpeedVac, and desalted using C18 ZipTips. LC-MS/MS was performed on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Easy-nLC 1200 UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using an Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 trapping column and an AUR3-25075C18, 25 cm × 75 µm, 1.7 µm C18 analytical column (IonOpticks). Peptides were eluted at a flow rate of 300 nL/min with a 106 min gradient from 3 to 28% solvent B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid), followed by a 15 min gradient from 28 to 44% solvent B and a short wash with 90% solvent B. Precursor scans were acquired from m/z 375 to 1,600 at a resolution of 120,000, and the most intense multiply charged precursors (charge states 2–8) were selected for fragmentation using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 27. MS/MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 15,000 with a 1.4 m/z isolation window and a 3 s cycle time. Dynamic exclusion was enabled for 30 s.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS/MS spectra were searched separately against the Araport11 database Arabidopsis thaliana (https://www.arabidopsis.org/), concatenated with decoy protein sequences using the MSFragger 4.1 software by including O-methylation at tyrosine (delta mass of +14.01565) as a variable modification with default criteria to obtain Label Free Quantitative (LFQ) intensities. The search results were analyzed separately in Perseus (version 2.0.10.0). The processing in Perseus was as follows: MSFragger intensities were log2-transformed. Only proteins that had at least three valid values in at least one group (WT or proUBQ10::sfGFPMfnG) were kept. The remaining missing MaxLFQ intensities were then imputed from a normal distribution that is downshifted by 1.8 and a width of 0.3 column-wise. A two-sample t-test was conducted with a permutation-based (n=250) FDR = 0.05 and S 0 = 1.5.
